headline: The second pathway
punch: It is not GH, and it has an approved drug.

headline: Everything so far
body: So every mechanism in this series has run through GH and IGF-1. That is the axis everyone argues about, it is genuinely central, and it deserves the attention it gets. | It is also not the only route into the growth plate. There is a second one with its own receptor, its own human genetics, and a drug that is already licensed and sitting in pharmacies. Almost nobody in this space talks about it, and the genetic evidence behind it is cleaner than anything on the GH side.
punch: There is more than one way into the plate.

headline: C-type natriuretic peptide
body: *CNP* acts on a receptor called **NPR2**, also written GC-B, which sits on the chondrocytes in your growth plate. It does not touch GH or IGF-1 anywhere in its chain. | It signals through cGMP, which activates *PKG*, which drives chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy on completely separate wiring. So this is not a modulator of the GH axis or a cofactor for it. It is a parallel system doing the same job by different means.
punch: A separate receptor. A separate second messenger.

headline: The genetics are unambiguous
body: Lose both working copies of NPR2 and you get **acromesomelic dysplasia**, a severe short-stature skeletal dysplasia. Gain-of-function mutations in the same gene produce skeletal overgrowth. | The dose of this single gene moves human height in both directions, which is about as clean as genetic evidence for a growth pathway ever gets. You rarely find a gene where breaking it and overdriving it both produce the predicted phenotype.
punch: _Break it, you are short. Overdrive it, you are tall._

headline: Olney 2006
body: They studied 39 members of a single family in which one person had the full dysplasia. Sixteen of those family members carried one broken copy of NPR2 and 23 did not. | The carriers had a height z-score of **-1.8**, against **-0.4** in the non-carriers, at P < 0.0005. One bad copy out of two cost roughly a standard deviation and a half of height. And there was **no difference in body proportion** between carriers and non-carriers, so they were simply shorter rather than oddly shaped.

headline: How common is that?
body: From carrier frequency the authors estimated that roughly **one in 30** people with idiopathic short stature carry an NPR2 mutation. | Idiopathic means nobody found a cause. So for a meaningful slice of people who were told there was no explanation for their height, there is one, and it sits in this pathway rather than in the GH axis everybody tested them for.
punch: Some unexplained short stature is this gene.

headline: The cross-link nobody mentions
body: Here is the finding that ties this whole series together. The family member with the full dysplasia had **low IGF-1 and evidence of GH resistance**, alongside very high circulating CNP. | A defect in the CNP receptor produced a growth hormone problem. These two pathways are not running in separate lanes and reporting separately. Break one badly enough and the other one reads as broken too, which should make you suspicious of any single-axis explanation.
punch: _Break the CNP receptor and the GH axis suffers too._

headline: And it is local again
body: Knock CNP out only in cartilage, leaving it intact everywhere else in the body, and the mice come out **almost as short as deleting it everywhere**. The same holds for its receptor. | What this means is that the CNP responsible for lengthening bone is manufactured inside the plate itself, not delivered there from the endothelium by the bloodstream. Which is precisely the lesson local IGF-1 taught, arrived at independently on a different pathway.

headline: What it does to the zones
body: In those cartilage-specific knockouts the **hypertrophic layer was drastically reduced** while the proliferative layer was only moderately reduced. | So CNP works mainly on the final swelling stage, which is the same stage Hunziker identified as the most efficient cellular contributor to bone elongation. Two independent lines of work pointing at hypertrophy as the biggest lever in the plate.
punch: It works on hypertrophy, the strongest lever.

headline: Why this beats FGFR3
body: *FGFR3* puts a brake on chondrocyte proliferation, and an overactive FGFR3 is what causes achondroplasia. The obvious drug target is FGFR3 itself, which is difficult and unselective. | But the cGMP arm of CNP signalling functionally antagonises that brake downstream. So you do not have to block FGFR3 at all. You can push the opposing pathway and release the brake from the other side, which is a much more tractable drug problem.
punch: Release the brake from the other side.

headline: Does pushing it actually work?
body: A CNP analogue given as a daily subcutaneous injection. Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, **121 children** with achondroplasia across 24 sites, 52 weeks of treatment. | Adjusted mean difference in annualised growth velocity: **1.57 cm per year** over placebo, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.93, p < 0.0001. That is a real randomised human result on a pathway that has nothing to do with growth hormone.
punch: _A randomised result on a second pathway._

headline: The caveat is theirs
body: Straight from the paper: **it is not known whether final adult height will be increased, or what the harms of long-term therapy might be**. | Growth velocity measured over one year is not adult height, and this series has made that exact point about GH several times already. It applies here identically and the authors said it themselves rather than waiting for someone else to point it out.

headline: What this changes
body: There are at least two independent routes into the growth plate, and both of them work through signals manufactured locally inside the tissue rather than delivered through circulation. | Which means a blood test reading one axis is reading even less of the overall picture than it looked like three posts ago, and the second axis has human genetics behind it that are cleaner than most of the first one.
punch: ==Two pathways. Both local. Neither on your bloodwork.==
